newsitem.title: USA: Disney execs to face tough questions at meeting.
newsitem.headline: Disney execs to face tough questions at meeting.

text.p: Like most companies, Walt Disney Co. has a few investors who come to the annual shareholders' meeting every year to grumble about the cost of a hamburger and fries at Walt Disney World or to offer advice about how to run the Magic Kingdom.
Normally, the gripes are easily deflected by Disney Chairman Michael Eisner and the shareholders leave, happy with the notion that their holdings are worth more today than they were a year ago.

But this year the normal grumbling is expected to sound more like a roaring lion as shareholders, upset with the millions of dollars Disney forked over to former President Michael Ovitz and the millions more it plans to pay Eisner, voice their concerns about how their money is being spent.

Unlike previous years when the criticism has come from a handful of individual investors seeking their 15 minutes of fame, the opposition at this year's meeting in Anaheim, Calif. on Tuesday will include a number of influential holders, including CalPERS, the giant California pension fund, and the College Retirement Equities Fund, which together hold about 11 million shares of Disney stock.

Both institutions have already vowed to oppose a controversial change in Eisner's compensation package and to withhold support for five Disney directors seeking re-election. While the moves are not likely to derail the measures, officials hope their actions will send a message to management that shareholders are unhappy with the way the company is being run.

"We have some major issues with Disney," a spokeswoman for the California Public Employees Retirement System said, pointing to the Ovitz settlement and Eisner's new contract. "We think the board is pretty much a rubber stamp and we want to see more independence on the board."

Last year, Disney awarded Ovitz, a former Hollywood talent agent, an estimated $93 million in cash and stock options to leave after about a year on the job. The move sparked a pair of lawsuits from angry shareholders who argued Ovitz did little to earn his money and that Disney's board of directors was caving in to Eisner's wishes.

"The payout to Michael Ovitz has set a troublesome precedent by giving a top officer an enormous severance package even though his work did not begin to match expectations, said Conrad MacKerron, director of social research for Progressive Asset Management, an Oakland, Calif.-based brokerage that specializes in socially responsible investing.
"We do not see how it was in the company's best interests to sign an employment agreement awarding Ovitz a vast sum of money in the event of his premature departure from the company."

Adding fuel to fire is a new 10-year contract for Eisner that could be worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Under the plan, which must be approved by shareholders, Eisner's base salary would remain at $750,000 a year. But he would also receive options for another eight million shares, which are hypothetically worth about $195 million, and a generous bonus based on Disney's performance. Currently, Eisner's stock options are worth an estimated $358 million.
Critics claim the compensation package is excessive.
"This is an enrichment package," the CalPERS spokeswoman said. "There needs to be a separation between management and the board."

Disney officials have defended the Ovitz settlement and the Eisner contract as the price for attracting and keeping talented executives at the helm. A number of entertainment companies have made changes at the executive level recently, and the settlement packages have been about the same as the one Ovitz received.

In the case of Eisner, Disney says shareholders need only to look at the company's stock price to see what he's done. Since 1984, when Eisner joined Disney, the company's stock has risen sharply, easily outperforming the Standard and Poors 500 index as well as Disney's peers in the entertainment industry.

Moreover, they note Disney's brand name is one of the best in the business and the company's ability to squeeze every nickel of profit from its movies and animated characters through cross-promotional activities is the envy of Hollywood.
But shareholders are starting to wonder if Eisner has too much power.

The College Retirement Equities Fund, which owns 7.4 million shares of Disney stock, said nine of the board's 16 directors are considered insiders rather than independent directors, raising questions about the board's decisions.

In a statement released Friday, the fund said it would vote against two Disney executive compensation plans and withhold support for the five directors up for re-election, including Walt Disney's nephew, Roy Disney.
